title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · Bonding and Structure

items.stem: The specification describes covalent bonding in terms of which particles?

options.text: ions which have swapped electron pairs
atoms sharing delocalised electrons
atoms which share pairs of electrons
electrons moving from atom to atom

items.why: This is the specification's wording: for covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons.

items.stem: Covalent bonding occurs in which of these?

options.text: compounds of non-metals only, never in elements
any compound made from two different elements
non-metals combined with metals in a lattice
most non-metallic elements and non-metal compounds

items.why: This is the specification statement: covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.

items.stem: Which ions have the electronic structure of a noble gas?

options.text: none, since an ion keeps its structure
those formed by Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7
only those whose charge equals the group
only metal ions, since they lose electrons

items.why: The specification names exactly these: ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

items.stem: Which pairing of group and ionic charge is correct?

options.text: Group 6 forms an ion carrying a 6- charge
Group 2 forms an ion with a charge of 2-
Group 7 forms a 7+ ion, from its group number
Group 6 forms an ion with a 2- charge

items.why: A Group 6 atom gains two electrons to reach a full outer shell, so the charge is 2-.

items.stem: What holds an ionic compound together?

options.text: strong bonds pointing from each ion to its partner
pairs of electrons shared between the ions
attraction between ions and loose electrons
strong electrostatic forces between charged ions

items.why: The specification states that ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

items.stem: Which pair of substances both have giant covalent structures?

options.text: carbon dioxide and silicon dioxide, two oxides
diamond and silicon dioxide, the named examples
poly(ethene) and diamond, both very large
sodium chloride and diamond, both giant

items.why: These are the two giant covalent structures given in the specification.

items.stem: How are the atoms arranged in a pure metal?

options.text: in a giant structure with a regular pattern
randomly, in a closely packed jumble of atoms
a lattice of positive and negative ions
in small groups of a few joined atoms

items.why: The specification states that metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

items.stem: In terms of electrostatic forces, what is the ionic bond in sodium chloride?

options.text: attraction between oppositely charged ions
the movement of an electron across the bond
a pair of electrons shared by the ions
attraction between the two atomic nuclei

items.why: Chemical bonding is explained by electrostatic forces; in an ionic compound these act between the positive and negative ions.

items.stem: Which statement correctly links the three bond types to what happens to the outer electrons?

options.text: ionic and metallic share electrons; covalent transfers
all three types involve sharing pairs of electrons
ionic transfers electrons; covalent and metallic share them
covalent shares electrons; ionic and metallic do not

items.why: Ionic bonding transfers electrons, covalent bonding shares pairs between atoms and metallic bonding shares delocalised electrons.

items.stem: A magnesium atom reacts with oxygen. What happens to magnesium's outer electrons?

options.text: six more are gained for a full outer shell
they are lost, giving a 2- charged ion
they are shared with the oxygen atom
they are transferred, giving a 2+ ion

items.why: Metal atoms lose the electrons in their outer shell and become positively charged ions.

items.stem: In a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride, how is the sodium ion drawn?

options.text: in brackets with a 1+ charge and one outer electron
with an arrow showing the electron crossing over
in brackets with a 1+ charge, outer shell empty
with one outer electron and no charge shown

items.why: The transferred electron is drawn in the chlorine outer shell, so it is not drawn on sodium as well.

items.stem: Why does the specification say that the forces in an ionic lattice act in all directions?

options.text: each ion is bonded to one partner ion only
the bonds point along fixed lines like sticks
each ion attracts oppositely charged ions around it
the ions only touch where the sticks join them

items.why: The attraction is between oppositely charged ions and is not confined to a line, so it holds the whole lattice together.

items.stem: Which of these is a limitation of a ball and stick model of sodium chloride?

options.text: the sticks suggest gaps between the ions
it shows the compound as separate molecules
it shows forces in two directions only
it cannot show a regular arrangement

items.why: In the real lattice the ions touch; the gaps and sticks exist only to make the arrangement visible.

items.stem: Water boils at 100 C. What does this tell you about the covalent bonds within a water molecule?

options.text: they are weak, since water boils easily
nothing; the bonds in it are strong
they break when the water turns to steam
they are weaker than ionic bonds are

items.why: Boiling separates whole molecules from each other. The bonds between atoms inside the molecule are strong and unaffected.

items.stem: Poly(ethene) is a covalently bonded substance with very large molecules. What does that mean?

options.text: its molecules are very large but separate
it has a giant covalent structure like diamond
the covalent bonds in it must be weaker
it is a mixture of very many small molecules

items.why: A polymer consists of very large molecules; each chain is a separate molecule.

items.stem: In the representation of a polymer, what does n stand for?

options.text: a number you work out from the diagram
the count of carbon atoms in the unit
the simplest whole number ratio of atoms
a large number of repeating units

items.why: The specification states only that n is a large number.

items.stem: In the displayed formula of methane, what does each of the four lines represent?

options.text: one electron passed from carbon to hydrogen
two bonds, one from each atom's own electron
a stick that holds the two atoms apart
one single bond, that is one shared pair

items.why: A line is used to represent a single covalent bond, which is one shared pair of electrons.

items.stem: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional displayed formula of a methane molecule?

options.text: it shows the atoms at their true relative size
it gives the ratio of atoms, not the number
it does not show the real shape of the molecule
it shows each bond as a single electron

items.why: A flat drawing cannot show that the four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

items.stem: Which statement about the electrons in a metal is correct?

options.text: each atom keeps its outer electrons, loosely
every electron in every atom is delocalised
the outer electrons are free to move about
the electrons are transferred to the ions

items.why: The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.

items.stem: In terms of electrostatic forces, what is a covalent bond?

options.text: attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei
attraction between the two positive nuclei
attraction between ions and delocalised electrons
an electron moving from one atom to the other

items.why: The shared pair of electrons is attracted to the nuclei of both bonded atoms, and that attraction is the bond.

items.stem: What gives rise to the strong metallic bonds in copper?

options.text: attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons
attraction between positive and negative ions
shared pairs of electrons between two metal atoms
each atom holding on to its own outer electrons

items.why: The sharing of delocalised electrons gives strong metallic bonds: the positive metal ions are attracted to the electrons.

items.stem: Which of these is a compound held together by ionic bonding?

options.text: lithium fluoride, a metal and a non-metal
sulfur dioxide, a compound of two elements
hydrogen chloride, a gas containing chloride
nitrogen gas, an element with very strong bonds

items.why: Lithium is a metal and fluorine a non-metal, which is exactly the condition the specification gives for ionic bonding.

items.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Which type of bonding does it have?

options.text: ionic, because it contains two different elements
metallic, because alloys bond like pure metals
ionic, since positive ions attract negative ions
covalent, as the atoms share outer electrons

items.why: The specification states that metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.

items.stem: A sodium atom, 2,8,1, forms a sodium ion. What is the ion's electronic structure and charge?

options.text: 2,8 with a charge of 1+, the same as neon
2,8,8 with a charge of 7-, like argon
2,8,1 with a 1+ charge, shells unchanged
2,8 but with a 1- charge, like neon

items.why: One outer electron is lost, leaving a full second shell and one more proton than electron.

items.stem: Which dot and cross diagram represents magnesium chloride?

options.text: one Mg2+ ion drawn with a single Cl- ion
one Mg2+ ion drawn with two Cl- ions
one Mg2+ ion drawn with a Cl7- ion
one Mg2- ion next to two Cl+ ions

items.why: Magnesium loses two electrons, one to each chlorine atom, so the ratio is one to two.

items.stem: Calcium is in Group 2 and fluorine in Group 7. Which pair of ions do they form?

options.text: Ca2+ and F-, since calcium loses two
Ca2+ and F7-, taken from the group numbers
Ca2- and F+, as calcium gains electrons
Ca2+ and F2-, so the formula is CaF

items.why: Group 2 metals lose two electrons to form 2+ ions; Group 7 non-metals gain one to form 1- ions.

items.stem: Potassium is in Group 1 and oxygen in Group 6. What is the formula of the compound formed?

options.text: KO, because one ion of each is enough
K2O, as two 1+ ions balance one 2- ion
K6O, read from the two group numbers
KO2, since oxygen forms two bonds

items.why: Potassium forms K+ and oxygen forms O2-, so two potassium ions are needed for each oxide ion.

items.stem: A diagram shows a regular cube of alternating small and large spheres, one element a metal. What is it?

options.text: separate molecules of the compound stacked up
a metal, its atoms in a random jumble
a giant covalent structure of shared pairs
a giant ionic lattice with the ions alternating

items.why: A regular alternating array of two elements, one a metal, is the giant ionic structure of a compound such as sodium chloride.

items.stem: A model of an ionic compound shows 8 magnesium ions and 16 chloride ions. What is the empirical formula?

options.text: Mg8Cl16, the numbers counted in the model
MgCl, since the ions pair up one to one
MgCl2, the simplest whole number ratio
Mg2Cl, with the larger number first

items.why: Eight to sixteen reduces to one to two, and an empirical formula is always the simplest ratio.

items.stem: Which of these substances consists of small molecules?

options.text: NaCl, a short two-symbol formula
SiO2, which looks just like CO2
CH4, a compound of two non-metals
MgO, a compound made of two elements

items.why: Carbon and hydrogen are both non-metals, and methane is one of the small molecules named in the specification.

items.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons are there between the atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?

options.text: two, drawn as four electrons in the overlap
one, since a covalent bond is one shared pair
four, one for each electron in the overlap
six, since each atom has six outer electrons

items.why: Each oxygen atom needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared: a double bond.

items.stem: A model of ethene shows two black balls (carbon), four white balls (hydrogen) and six sticks. What is the molecular formula?

options.text: CH2, the simplest whole number ratio
C2H4, counting only the balls
C2H6, one hydrogen for each stick
C6H4, taking the sticks as carbons

items.why: The molecular formula counts the atoms shown: two carbon and four hydrogen.

items.stem: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?

options.text: At its melting point, the same value as for melting
At its freezing point, a lower value than melting
At its boiling point, where condensing happens
At any temperature far below room warmth

items.why: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point.

items.stem: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?

options.text: As spheres drawn to the true size of an atom
As spheres that swell when the solid melts
As small solid spheres of the same kind
As tiny cubes stacked in a neat grid

items.why: The specification states that in this model particles are represented by small solid spheres.

items.stem: (HT only) Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the three states of matter?

options.text: The model draws far too few particles to be realistic
The model cannot explain any melting or boiling at all
The model shows solid, liquid and gas apart
The model shows no forces between the particles

items.why: The specification lists the absence of forces as one of the limitations of the simple model.

items.stem: What does the state symbol (aq) tell you about a substance in an equation?

options.text: It is a liquid, whether or not it is water
It is the water used as the solvent here
It is a gas bubbled through the mixture
It is dissolved in water to give a solution

items.why: (aq) shows an aqueous solution, that is a substance dissolved in water.

items.stem: Which statement about a substance made of small molecules is correct?

options.text: Covalent bonds are the weakest forces in the substance
Intermolecular forces act inside each molecule
Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds
There are no forces at all between the molecules

items.why: The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak compared with the covalent bonds inside them.

items.stem: Why do some substances need much more energy to boil than others?

options.text: Because the particles they contain are larger and heavier
Because they have to be heated for a much longer time
Because the forces between their particles are stronger
Because a greater mass of substance is being used

items.why: The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.

items.stem: (HT only) In the simple model the particles are solid inelastic spheres with no forces between them. Why does this make boiling hard to explain?

options.text: Boiling overcomes forces the model leaves out
The spheres are drawn much larger than real atoms
The model uses far fewer particles than a real sample
The particles in the model move much too slowly

items.why: Energy is needed at the boiling point to overcome forces between particles, and the model contains no forces.

items.stem: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C but chlorine melts at -101 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?

options.text: Sodium chloride has strong ionic attractions to break
The covalent bonds inside chlorine break easily as it melts
Chlorine has fewer bonds, so it melts a lot sooner
Sodium chloride particles are much heavier than chlorine

items.why: Different bonding gives forces of very different strengths, so far more energy is needed to melt the ionic lattice.

items.stem: A student says that one copper atom is shiny, can be bent and conducts electricity. Why is this wrong?

options.text: A single atom is shiny but it cannot conduct
Bulk properties belong to whole structures
Only atoms that are inside a compound gain them
An atom is too small to see, so nothing is known

items.why: Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity come from very many atoms arranged and bonded together.

items.stem: Why is sodium chloride described as a giant ionic lattice?

options.text: It is built from millions of NaCl molecules joined up
Every sodium ion is attracted to just one chloride ion
Very many ions sit in a regular repeating pattern
The electrostatic forces act along the rows of ions

items.why: An ionic compound has a regular structure in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in all directions.

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and boiling points?

options.text: Breaking the many strong bonds needs large amounts of energy
The ions are heavy and packed so tightly they cannot move
Every ion in the lattice repels the ions beside it
The ions must be split into atoms before it can melt

items.why: This is the reason given by the specification for the high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds.

items.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?

options.text: Melting releases electrons that can move through the liquid
In the liquid the ions are free to move and carry charge
Melting turns the neutral particles into charged ions
Liquids conduct just like water does, but solids never can

items.why: When melted, the ions are no longer held in fixed positions, so charge can flow.

items.stem: Sodium chloride is dissolved in water. Why does the solution conduct electricity?

options.text: Water itself is a very good conductor of electricity
Dissolving splits the molecules into atoms
The ions separate and are free to move about
The water supplies free electrons to the mixture

items.why: Dissolving frees the ions from the lattice so that charge can flow.

items.stem: Why are substances made of small molecules usually gases or liquids at room temperature?

options.text: Their covalent bonds are weak and break very easily
Their molecules are light enough to float away
There are no forces at all between the molecules
Only weak forces hold the molecules together

items.why: Substances made of small molecules have only weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

items.stem: When liquid water boils, what is overcome?

options.text: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
The intermolecular forces between the water molecules
Both the covalent bonds and the forces between them
The molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen

items.why: It is the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a substance boils.

items.stem: Why does liquid octane not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its molecules have no overall electric charge
It has no metal atoms to carry the charge along
Liquids are not able to conduct electricity at all
Its electrons are locked inside the atoms themselves

items.why: Conduction needs charged particles free to move, and molecules are neutral overall.

items.stem: The bonds inside a Cl2 molecule are strong, yet chlorine boils at -34 degrees C. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The strong covalent bonds break as the chlorine boils
Some covalent bonds break and some are left whole
Boiling only has to overcome weak forces between molecules
Chlorine molecules have nothing holding them close

items.why: The strong covalent bonds are not broken; only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

items.stem: Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature?

options.text: Covalent bonds join each polymer chain to the next one
It is a giant covalent structure just like diamond
Its molecules are far too heavy to move at all
Its very large molecules attract each other strongly

items.why: Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong.

items.stem: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?

options.text: Its intermolecular forces are very strong
Strong covalent bonds must be overcome
Strong forces hold its oppositely charged ions
Its atoms are heavy and hard to pull apart

items.why: All the atoms in a giant covalent structure are linked by strong covalent bonds, which must be overcome to melt it.

items.stem: Why do most metals have high melting points and boiling points?

options.text: The metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong
The atoms in a metal are heavy and packed very tightly
Metals are hard, and hard materials melt slowly
Delocalised electrons stop the atoms escaping

items.why: Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding, so most have high melting and boiling points.

items.stem: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?

options.text: The two metals react to make a new compound entirely
Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding
The alloy contains far more delocalised electrons
The added atoms are heavier and much harder

items.why: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers that can slide; different sized atoms disrupt those layers.

items.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity and of thermal energy?

options.text: The metal ions are free to move around the metal
The atoms are packed so tightly that energy passes
Delocalised electrons carry charge and energy
Protons in the metal carry the electric charge along

items.why: The delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal and also transfer thermal energy.

items.stem: Bromine vapour is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which change of state is this, and at which temperature does it happen?

options.text: Condensing, at the condensing point of bromine
Condensing, at the boiling point of bromine
Freezing, at the melting point of bromine
Condensing, at bromine's melting point

items.why: Boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.

items.stem: A solid is heated until it melts. Using the simple particle model, what happens to the particles?

options.text: They soften and change into smaller spheres
They break up into several smaller particles
They lose their shape and flow into each other
They stay the same but move further apart

items.why: A change of state alters the arrangement and movement of the particles, not the particles themselves.

items.stem: Substance X melts at 801 degrees C and substance Y melts at -7 degrees C. What does this tell you about the two substances?

options.text: The particles in X must be much heavier than in Y
The forces between the particles in X are much stronger
Substance Y has no forces between its particles
Y has stronger forces, so it melts much sooner

items.why: The stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting point.

items.stem: Ethanol melts at -114 degrees C and boils at 78 degrees C. What is the state of ethanol at 25 degrees C?

options.text: Gas, because 25 degrees C is above the melting point
Solid, because 25 degrees C is far below 78 degrees
Liquid, because 25 degrees C lies between the two values
Liquid and gas together in about equal amounts

items.why: A substance is a liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.

items.stem: Substance P has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. What is the state of P at 20 degrees C?

options.text: Liquid, since 20 degrees C is above its melting point
Solid, because both quoted values are below zero
Liquid, which is normal at room temperature
Gas, since 20 degrees C is above its boiling point

items.why: Above the boiling point the substance is a gas, whatever sign the quoted values carry.

items.stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?

options.text: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)
Mg(s) + 2HCl(l) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)

items.why: The metal is solid, the acid and the salt are dissolved in water, and hydrogen is given off as a gas.

items.stem: Calcium carbonate chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?

options.text: CaCO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(l) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

items.why: The chips are solid, the acid and the salt are aqueous, the water is a pure liquid and carbon dioxide is a gas.

items.stem: Methane, CH4, boils at -162 degrees C while octane, C8H18, boils at 126 degrees C. Why is octane's boiling point so much higher?

options.text: Octane molecules are heavier, so they need more heat energy
Octane has more covalent bonds that must be broken first
Octane is a liquid, and liquids always boil high
Its molecules are larger, so the forces are stronger

items.why: Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.

items.stem: A diagram shows a long chain of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with the chain continuing at both ends. What does it show?

options.text: A polymer built from large molecules
A giant covalent structure such as silica
A metal, since the atoms lie in a line
A small molecule such as ethene gas

items.why: Continuation marks and a repeating covalently bonded chain identify a polymer molecule.

items.stem: A diagram shows every carbon atom bonded to four other carbon atoms in a continuous network. What does the diagram show?

options.text: A very large molecule of carbon, like C60
A giant metallic lattice of carbon atoms
A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A giant covalent structure, such as diamond

items.why: Every atom linked to other atoms by covalent bonds throughout the structure identifies a giant covalent structure.
